gameplay_summary: Vertical-scrolling helicopter shooter: fire short-range shots at tanks, boats and turrets, use two screen-clearing bombs that also act as a shield, and pick up side-helicopter helpers from flashing panels.
dossier: Toaplan's first shooter, a 1985 arcade game released by Taito, ported to Famicom by Micronics. Your attack helicopter has a forward shot with limited range, plus two bombs mounted on its sides. A bomb clears enemies and bullets in a radius, and if an enemy bullet hits a mounted bomb it detonates automatically, which saves you. Ground panels flash white, red and green; destroy one on a given colour to get a forward-firing helper helicopter, a side-firing helper, or a bomb refill. Up to two helpers can fly with you. Its focus on ground targets set the template for Toaplan's later shooters.

nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Tiger-Heli, published in North America by Acclaim (1987) rather than Pony Canyon.

gameplay_summary: Run-and-gun platformer: as Ultra Magnus, shoot through ten horizontal and vertical stages of Decepticons, switching between robot mode and car-carrier mode, with a boss at the end of each.
dossier: Takara's first Famicom game, sold on the mystery of who killed Convoy (Optimus Prime). The 1986 film hadn't yet been released in Japan, so Japanese fans didn't know. Ultra Magnus fights through ten stages across three eras of the cartoon, travelling by time tunnel. Robot mode jumps and shoots forward; vehicle mode keeps low and fires up and forward but can't jump, and some vertical stages need both. One hit kills you, so it's extremely hard. Bosses are large Decepticons. Collecting the R-O-D-I-M-U-S letter marks through the game turns you into Rodimus Convoy on the next loop. A hidden continue code is a near-necessity. The game misspells Convoy as 'Comvoy'.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action game; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Space war strategy: develop star systems and command fleets in turn-based ship battles against Shiva-Rudra's forces in a Hindu-mythology space opera.
dossier: T&E Soft's DAIVA was a seven-story space opera spread across seven platforms, each one telling a different chapter, inspired by Hindu mythology. Fleet data could be carried between versions by password. This Famicom chapter is a simplified take on the series. You build up planets and fleets and fight turn-based battles by placing ships and trading fire, with a chance to retreat every few turns, as the story moves toward the twin planets of Nirsartia. The ja.wikipedia series article notes the Famicom version lacks parts of the PC versions' system, such as morale. It is one of the earlier console space-strategy games, though few people played it.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Menu-driven strategy whose commands, reports and story are Japanese text; progress depends on understanding them.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Dig Dug-style digging game: tunnel through underground levels to find the keys behind four doors, then the exit, avoiding monsters and spurting lava and using items like dynamite and a wetsuit.
dossier: A Use Corporation digging game in the vein of Dig Dug, without the falling rocks. Hottaaman burrows through each level's earth to find keys behind four doors and then the door to the next level. Items add variety: teleporting doors, speed-ups, dynamite, and a wetsuit for flooded areas. Lava can spurt upward and kill you, and it stays where it is after you lose a life, so it is a lasting hazard within a game. There are 15 levels, which then repeat, and a password system activated by a button combination. It's an obscure, budget-feeling title.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action game; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Arcade-style baseball with distinct teams and players: pitch with speed and movement, swing with timing, and field and run the bases in a quick game against the computer or a friend.
dossier: Namco's first Famista, the game that redefined Famicom baseball and sold over two million copies. Developer Yoshihiro Kishimoto built it after playing Nintendo's Baseball and wishing players had names and abilities. Here every player is distinct, with batting averages, power, speed and pitching stats, so line-ups and pinch-hitters matter. It's still quick and arcade-like to play: control a pitcher's speed and curve, time swings, and field with simple controls. The teams are parodies of the Japanese pro league. Its sequels became a yearly Japanese institution. Tengen released it in North America as R.B.I. Baseball, with MLB player data.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Standard baseball; player names are katakana, but nothing needs reading to play.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as R.B.I. Baseball (1988), published by Tengen with MLB players.
japanese_version_notes: Teams and players are parodies of the Japanese professional league; R.B.I. Baseball replaced them with licensed MLB player data.

gameplay_summary: Absurd action-adventure designed by Beat Takeshi: as a fed-up salaryman, quit your job, divorce your wife, gather skills and money, then fly to a South Seas island to find buried treasure.
dossier: Comedian and director Takeshi Kitano's notorious game, ranked the worst ever by Famitsu readers and long a byword for kusoge. You play a broke salaryman in a grubby, yakuza-filled town who gets a treasure map. To go after it you must cut every tie: quit, divorce, get qualifications, then travel to Hintabo Island and fly a hang-glider shooting section to reach the treasure. Progress depends on bizarre, unhinted actions, such as singing karaoke into the Famicom's controller II microphone. Choosing the wrong flight blows up your plane, and many choices end with your own funeral. You can also beat up passers-by. It's a deliberate prank on players, now treated as a cult artefact.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Progress hinges on reading Japanese dialogue and choices and on understanding bizarre instructions; even Japanese players needed a guide.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Uses the Famicom controller II microphone for one key action, which an NES-style controller can't do.

gameplay_summary: Action-adventure: as Sherlock Holmes, roam London and Britain fighting armed thugs, gathering clues, money and items, to rescue Earl Apple's kidnapped daughter Margaret from the Papaya gang.
dossier: Towa Chiki's first game, released ahead of the Holmes centenary and remembered as a violent oddity. Holmes is dropped into London with no explanation and spends most of his time fighting: kicking thugs, armed passers-by and even innocent citizens, often before they'll talk. Fallen enemies drop money, and knives and guns can be picked up. Examining objects needs a magnifying glass that you don't start with, and nothing tells you so. Clues from parks, sewers and houses point the way to the kidnapper. If Holmes dies, the case goes unsolved and the game ends. An unofficial English translation patch exists.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — The investigation runs on Japanese dialogue and clues; the fighting is visual, but you can't follow the case without reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Three-world Doraemon action game: rescue Nobita and friends across space, a jungle 'demon realm' and the sea floor, each world using a different game style, collecting dorayaki and gadgets.
dossier: Hudson's 1.15-million-selling Doraemon game, nicknamed 'Shiro-Dora' after its white cartridge. A time machine accident has scattered the gang and Doraemon's gadgets across three worlds drawn from the early films (Space Pioneer, the Great Demon realm and the Undersea Fortress). Each world plays very differently, almost like three games in one, including an overhead world, a side-scrolling platform world where Gian and Suneo help as options, and an undersea shooting world. Dorayaki restore health and gadgets power you up. A continue trick and world-select codes exist. Sources agree it's playable without Japanese.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action throughout; English-language sources note it is playable without Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Overhead action RPG: as Prince Myer, explore a field and seven towers throwing swords at monsters, buy items, find hidden rooms, and burn each tower's magic bell in the sacred flame.
dossier: An Irem action RPG, sold abroad as Deadly Towers; it was meant to be called Hell's Bells but couldn't use that name. The demon Rubas is using seven bells to summon monsters, and Prince Myer must take each bell from its tower's boss and burn it in the holy flame before facing Rubas. You attack by throwing your sword, one at a time. Health is a life meter, and falling off ambiguous cliff edges ends the game outright. Burning bells makes enemies tougher, and once a tower's bell is taken you can't go back in for missed hidden items. Shops sell gear, and hidden rooms are everywhere. It's infamous in the West for its difficulty and stiffness. The Japanese cartridge has a red LED.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action-based; the little shop text isn't needed to progress, and the obscure hidden rooms are the same in any language.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Deadly Towers (1987).
japanese_version_notes: The Famicom cartridge has a red LED, matching the title's pun (mashou: 'evil bell' / 'devilish').

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling obstacle sprint: run a runner down a trap-filled corridor, jumping hurdles and slow tiles and riding skateboards and springboards, to reach the goal before the timer runs out.
dossier: A port of Namco's 1985 arcade game, a pure reflex race against the clock. The runner sprints right down a tiled corridor full of obstacles: green tiles that slow you, hurdles, rolling cans, and giant tyres. Jumping costs a fraction of a second compared with running, so the challenge is finding a fast line and knowing when to leap. Skateboards and springboard 'cracker' jumps speed you along, and drink cans along the way are worth points. There are 32 rounds in eight stages of four, and the time left from the first three rounds of a stage carries into the fourth. It is short, sharp and tough.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; this Famicom port was released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Overhead flip-screen action based on King Kong Lives: as Kong, punch, stomp and throw rocks through nine maze-like worlds, smashing scenery to find hidden doors, to rescue Lady Kong.
dossier: Konami's game of the 1986 film King Kong Lives (King Kong 2 in Japan). Kong has escaped the lab and is looking for the captive Lady Kong across nine overhead 'worlds' of military bases, jungles, mountains, cities and underground areas. He punches, stomps (which some enemies resist) and throws rocks in an arc; Select switches between punch and rocks. Smashing the landscape reveals hidden items and doorways, which is how you find the route onward. Water slows you, stops you jumping and drains health. After the ending, the game loops. The film's human characters don't appear.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action game; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling action RPG: as the sword-and-sorcery heroine Lucia, explore each stage for the orb that opens the next door, using six spells and items that raise your HP and MP.
dossier: A Sunsoft action game from the 1986 wave of early Famicom heroine games. Lucia, the only magic user of her clan, must recover the Wing of Madoola statue from the traitor Darutos. Each stage is a maze-like area, and you find the jewel that unlocks the next door. Along the way, items raise her HP, MP and sword power. She swings a sword and casts six spells, selected with Start and Select, each costing MP. Running out of MP only stops your magic, but running out of HP ends the game. It's challenging and explorative, with a keyword prize campaign at the time. It got an official English release on a 2024 Sunsoft compilation.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action game with English status labels; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling run and gun across eight asteroids: as special-forces agent Layla, shoot through surface and base sections with weapons from boxes, rescue partner Iris, and beat the boss of each base.
dossier: A dB-SOFT action game in the style of the Dirty Pair anime, and one of the early Famicom 'heroine' games. Layla, of the CAT special forces, must destroy Dr. Manitoka's gene machine and rescue her kidnapped partner Iris. Each asteroid has a surface part, including a space-bike shooting section, and a cavern-like base, scrolling one way only. Weapon boxes upgrade her starting handgun, and a roller-skate item speeds her up. Lingering too long summons a tornado enemy. Falling into pits costs health and items rather than a life. Once rescued, Iris follows a step behind and mirrors Layla's shots, sharing her ammo. Password disks are collected along the way.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action game; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Floor-mat track and field: run in place on the Family Trainer mat to power a runner through the 100 m dash, 110 m hurdles, long jump and triple jump, alone or racing a second player.
dossier: The second Family Trainer game, using the mat's 12-sensor side. The view changes from Athletic World's side view to one looking down the track behind your runner, so your stepping direction matches the screen. There are four events: 100 m dash, 110 m hurdles, long jump and triple jump. Speed comes from how fast you step, which row of pads you use sets your top speed, and lifting your feet before the gun is a false start. Tournament mode races you against the computer or a second player in the sprint and hurdles, while Olympic mode runs all four events with bronze, silver and gold qualifying marks. In North America it was first sold by Bandai as Stadium Events, now one of the rarest NES cartridges, then reissued by Nintendo as World Class Track Meet.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Physical play on the mat; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Stadium Events (Bandai, 1987), then reissued by Nintendo as World Class Track Meet (1988) for the Power Pad.
japanese_version_notes: Requires the Family Trainer mat, which plugs into the Famicom expansion port; the NES Power Pad won't connect without an adapter.

gameplay_summary: First-person cockpit space combat: warp around a sector map to wipe out enemy fleets before they surround the refugee ship CosmoStation Noah, visiting planets and stations for upgrades and repairs.
dossier: ASCII's cockpit-view space shooter, in the Star Raiders mould like Namco's Star Luster. A fleet of space terrorists is closing in on the refugee transport CosmoStation Noah, which stays put while you hunt them down. The galaxy is a grid of sub-spaces: you jump between them, fight enemy craft in first person, and plan your route before the fleets converge. Up to eight planets offer engine and weapon upgrades, space stations repair you, and there's an asteroid field and a black hole that is hard but not impossible to escape. You win by clearing every enemy fleet in time. The development name was reportedly '3D Uga Uga'.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The combat is visual, but the Famicom version's status and planet/station text is Japanese (the NES version is in English), and the upgrade system is easier to follow if you can read it.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Star Voyager (1987), published by Acclaim.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling hack and slash: as Ryu, advance through post-apocalyptic ruins with a sword and shield, blocking and slashing past enemies to beat each stage's boss; lose the shield and you fight with fists.
dossier: Capcom's 1986 arcade game directed by Takashi Nishiyama, a spiritual successor to Kung-Fu Master and close in feel to Ghosts 'n Goblins. In a world ruined by nuclear war and ruled by an evil warlord's army, the hero fights with a sword and shield. One button slashes and the other blocks, and blocking well is the core skill. Certain attacks knock the shield away; then the two buttons become punch and kick. The characters are large sprites and the stages have few gimmicks; the danger is the enemies. Health only refills at stage clears or from rare winged-heart pickups. There are six stages, played through twice.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action game; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Trojan (1987).

gameplay_summary: Licensed action-adventure starring the rock band Seikima-II: as Demon Kogure, explore five stages to free the captured band members, buy the instruments you need, and retrieve the devil's scripture from the god Zeus.
dossier: A CBS Sony game built around the heavy-metal band Seikima-II, whose members play as demons. Demon Kogure must rescue his bandmates from Zeus and hold a 'Black Mass' concert. Each of the five stages hides a captured member behind a gatekeeper with a key. Each also sells an instrument you must buy; miss any and the concert fails, giving the bad ending. The LIFE counter works as a timer that drains constantly and drops further when you're hit, and drinking blood refills it. Collected money buys weapon upgrades from stones up to bats. A hidden continue exists, but using it wipes your instruments, so a continued run can only reach the bad ending. Critics noted it closely resembles Dragon Slayer IV with the characters swapped.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action-based; the shop and instrument items aren't hard to work out, and nothing else needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Block breaker: move the Vaus paddle to bounce the energy ball into walls of bricks, catching falling capsules for power-ups such as lasers, a wider paddle or multiple balls, until you reach DOH.
dossier: Taito's 1986 arcade hit, which revived Breakout and set the template for the genre. You guard the bottom of the screen with the Vaus paddle and clear each round's bricks. Some bricks need several hits and others can't be broken at all. Capsules fall from broken bricks: lasers, an extended paddle, a catch ability, slowing, splitting the ball into three, an exit warp, and extra lives. Floating enemies deflect the ball unpredictably. The final round is a fight with DOH, the giant head behind it all. The Famicom version came with Taito's own paddle (dial) controller, which gives the precise control the game needs; the standard pad is far worse.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade action with English text; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Arkanoid (North America 1987).
japanese_version_notes: Packaged with the Famicom Arkanoid paddle (dial controller), which plugs into the Famicom expansion port; the NES Arkanoid controller uses a different connector.

gameplay_summary: Time-travel adventure based on the anime film: travel through Japanese history answering yes/no questions from figures like Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, steering history toward a peaceful future.
dossier: Kemco's game for the 1986 anime film Toki no Tabibito, released a week after the film. It keeps little of the film's plot, though. Kutajima Toshito, worried about a future of nuclear war, travels back in time to change human history. Progress is a chain of yes/no answers to historical figures. A wrong answer can bounce you to an earlier era or a different history, or get you cut down, shot, beaten, or choked on rice cake, all depicted memorably. Missing the time machine COI or letting it run out of fuel also ends the game. Multiple endings show different histories, such as one ruled by money and one ruled by force.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Everything hinges on understanding Japanese questions and story text to choose yes or no; guessing gets you killed.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Skyscraper-climbing action: work the climber's left and right arms separately to haul him up the face of a building, dodging closing windows, falling objects, a giant gorilla and other hazards.
dossier: Nichibutsu's 1980 arcade original, one of the first 'climbing games', designed by Shigeki Fujiwara, who later created Bomberman at Hudson. In the arcade, two joysticks control the climber's two arms: raise one to grab a window ledge, pull down to lift the body, and alternate in rhythm to climb. Windows slide shut on your hands, residents drop flowerpots, a condor drops things on you, signs fall, and a King Kong-like gorilla swats at you, until you reach the helicopter on the roof. The Famicom version recreates the twin-stick control with the bundled 'Climber Sticks' and adds more stages than the arcade's four.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Arcade action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; this Famicom version was released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Packaged with Climber Sticks, which recreate the arcade's twin-joystick control on the Famicom.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling action platformer: as the sculptor Gaou, travel through different eras throwing chisels at enemies and placing demon-tile blocks as platforms, to recover the 16 fragments of a stolen phoenix carving.
dossier: Konami's game based on Osamu Tezuka's Phoenix (the Karma chapter's 1986 anime film), the first Famicom release of 1987. It uses the story loosely. Gaou, a former bandit turned Buddhist sculptor, must recover his phoenix carving, which has been split into 16 pieces and scattered through time. You attack by throwing chisels, which have short range, forward or straight up. The hook is the onigawara, demon-faced roof tiles that you can set down as blocks to climb on or break, and you need to manage them to get through the stages. Most of the 16 stages end with a boss guarding a fragment; some are trap gauntlets instead. If you run out of tiles and get stuck, Select self-destructs.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Platform action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Side-view action RPG: as the swordsman Clovis, pick a route across a round map, fight through monster-filled dungeons to find each exit, and slay the dragon at Dragon Mountain to rescue Princess Celia.
dossier: A Tose port of Namco's 1985 arcade game. Each round opens on a map where you choose a path of dungeons to Dragon Mountain. Dungeons are side-view mazes with roaming monsters and room guardians, plus a timer: stay too long and the music changes as a cave shark comes hunting you. Clovis fights with a sword and has a double jump and a downward thrust from mid-air. Experience raises his vitality, and the Famicom version adds about 20 items, including magic and utility items and a thief who can steal your super sword. There are 12 rounds; the ending shows a code for 'Ura Dragon Buster', a much harder second quest. It's an early, influential action RPG.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action game with English labels; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; this Famicom port was released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Licensed maze action game based on the film Labyrinth: guide the heroine through warping, trap-filled mazes to reach the Goblin King's castle and rescue her brother Toby within 13 hours.
dossier: A Tokuma Shoten action game developed by Atlus, with Kouji Okada designing and Tsukasa Masuko composing. It follows the film's premise: Jareth has taken baby Toby, and you have 13 hours to get through the Labyrinth to his castle. The game is a series of tricky maze areas. Some warp you around, some reverse the D-pad, and some drain the clock at high speed. Playing in the wrong order can leave you unable to reach new areas. The music uses songs from the film, including Magic Dance and Chilly Down. It's a different game from the Lucasfilm/Activision computer game of the same film.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The mazes are visual, but item and event text appears in Japanese, and progression is opaque enough that reading helps.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. It is a different game from the Activision computer game Labyrinth.

gameplay_summary: Turn-based party RPG: as Erdrick's descendant, the prince of Midenhall, recruit two royal cousins, explore a much larger world by land and sea, and stop the sorcerer Hargon.
dossier: The second Dragon Quest, set 100 years after the first. Its launch-day queues helped spark the Dragon Quest phenomenon. The prince of Midenhall (Lorasia) teams up with the prince of Cannock (Sumaltria), a light fighter-caster, and the princess of Moonbrooke, a magic user. That makes this the first game in the series with a party and multi-enemy battles. The world is over six times larger than the first game's, and later you sail freely by ship. Many of its systems carried on through the series. It's long and notoriously hard, especially the late dungeons and Hargon's final fights. Progress is saved with a long kana password.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Text-driven RPG: dialogue, menus and the long kana passwords are Japanese, and clues from townspeople matter for finding key items.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Dragon Warrior II (1990).
japanese_version_notes: Progress is kept with long passwords (fukkatsu no jumon); the NES Dragon Warrior II saves to a battery instead, and adds a story introduction in Moonbrooke that the Japanese original lacks. The North American release also used archaic-style English and censored some religious imagery.

gameplay_summary: Bass-fishing simulation: choose a spot on the lake, cast your lure with the right power, work it to attract a fish, and reel it in without snapping the line, catching as many black bass as possible between sunrise and sunset.
dossier: Hot-B's Famicom version of its 1984 PC-88 game, the root of the long Super Black Bass series. A day on the lake runs from sunrise to sunset. You pick a spot, cast, then twitch and drag the lure to tempt a bite. Once hooked, a bass fights back, and reeling constantly breaks the line and loses both fish and lure. Between casts you can change position and tackle. A beginner's game lets you just fish, while the ranking game is entered with a password. It's a slow, quiet simulation for fishing fans.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Casting and reeling are visual, but the menus for tackle, locations and the ranking password are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; this Famicom version was released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Prehistoric vertical-scrolling action shooter: as caveman hero Max, walk and jump up the screen past dinosaurs and pits, throwing weapons that upgrade from rocks to axes and beyond, and beat each stage's boss.
dossier: A Hudson game sold under the Rix Soft brand, which Hudson set up with Ricoh to get around Nintendo's limit of five Famicom releases per year for each publisher. It is a vertically scrolling shooter on foot: you move freely, jump pits and gaps, and throw weapons at prehistoric enemies. Hitting boulders reveals power-ups such as faster movement, wings for flight, and weapon upgrades from rocks through stone axes to boomerangs and beyond. The game is a tie-in with pro wrestler Riki Choshu: a special item turns Max into 'Riki', who throws clones of himself in Choshu's Riki Lariat pose. The name Shinjinrui ('new humans') was the 1986 buzzword of the year. The girl on the box doesn't appear in the game.

nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Adventures of Dino Riki (1989).
japanese_version_notes: The Riki Choshu wrestling tie-in, with the Riki transformation and lariat attack, is central to the Japanese release; the NES version kept the Riki name for its hero.

gameplay_summary: Martial-arts action in two styles: side-scrolling journey stages where Ryuhi fights through enemies and bosses to find items, alternating with one-on-one tournament bouts in a world fighting championship.

After training at Shaolin, Ryuhi enters an inter-style world tournament to get them back. Play Studio turns the mat into a keyboard for free play, has you step out melodies such as 'Neko Funjatta', and offers step drills without music. language_barrier_reason: LOW — Follow-the-instructor movement; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Dance Aerobics (1989), for the Power Pad.
japanese_version_notes: Requires the Family Trainer mat, which plugs into the Famicom expansion port; the NES Power Pad won't connect without an adapter.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling time-travel action: as Hashimoto-saurus, a dinosaur-ised version of Bandai's game ambassador Hashimoto Meijin, travel through eras fighting monsters to defeat the time emperor Salamander and get his body back.
dossier: Bandai's game based on its 'Pocket Zaurus' dinosaur stationery line, starring its own celebrity gamer Hashimoto Meijin, turned into a dinosaur by the villain Salamander's curse. language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The action is visual, but hints and the quiz sections rely on Japanese text in the message window.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Music software: play notes along with backing tracks using the controller, letting you perform and make music without instrument skills.
dossier: A Tokyo Shoseki music title developed by Musical Plan. The ja.wikipedia master list describes it as a music game in which you make sounds along with background music, and notes it was first announced as 'Family Synth Music World'. FamiWiki calls it music creation software, and some of its tracks were reused in a later web series. nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Licensed action platformer: as Mickey, with Minnie following behind, travel through Alice in Wonderland-themed worlds, shooting stars at enemies and searching doors and hidden spots for items.
dossier: Hudson's Mickey Mouse game, the first Disney game on the Famicom. The title screen just says Mickey Mouse, so in Japan it's often called 'Hudson's Mickey'. Mickey travels with Minnie trailing behind him. The stages are built around an Alice in Wonderland theme. Like Hudson's Doraemon game, each world has its own layout and feel, and the score and life displays look similar. Capcom published it in North America as Mickey Mousecapade, which sold over a million copies, with many enemies, items, weapons, bosses and level names changed.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Platform action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Mickey Mousecapade (1988), an altered version with different enemies, items and bosses.
japanese_version_notes: The Japanese original's enemies, items, weapons, bosses and level names differ from those in the North American Mickey Mousecapade.

gameplay_summary: Western conversation game: as the sheriff, face a series of townsfolk on the main street, pick your replies in each conversation, and draw your gun on outlaws, robbers and anyone who pulls on you.
dossier: A Pony Canyon port of Accolade's 1985 computer game, the only Accolade game designed by co-founder Alan Miller. You see the street over the sheriff's shoulder as 11 characters come up to talk: the doctor, a schoolmarm, gamblers, outlaws and others. Each line gets a choice of replies, and good conversations score points. Pick badly and the person may draw on you; a hidden gunman may also shoot whoever you're talking to. Pressing up beyond the top reply draws your gun, letting you shoot outlaws, bank robbers or hidden money bags, but shooting the person you're talking to zeroes your score. Two wounds and you're done. The Famicom text is known for its many typos.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Choosing the right replies depends on reading Japanese dialogue; the shooting is only part of it.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; the Famicom version was released only in Japan. The original is an American computer game.

gameplay_summary: Licensed action game based on the baseball manga Touch: the twins Tatsuya and Kazuya and their friend Minami travel to another dimension to rescue ten puppies, punching and throwing baseballs at enemies.
dossier: A Compile-developed game for Toho, based on Mitsuru Adachi's hugely popular high-school baseball manga, but with no baseball beyond throwing balls. The dog Punch's ten puppies have fallen into another dimension, and the Uesugi twins and Minami go after them, fighting strange enemies by punching and throwing baseballs. Minami has zero attack power and mostly tags along, while you roam large fields full of many tough enemies. It has a reputation for difficulty, and a well-known cheat starts Tatsuya with endgame-strength stats. It's for fans of the license.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action-based; nothing needs reading to play.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Showbiz action game: control two aspiring idols at once, moving together and spreading apart with up and down, freezing enemies with 'charisma wave' songs and squashing them between the pair.
dossier: A Victor Musical Industries action game about two 17-year-olds from Hakata and Hiroshima who form a duo and go to Tokyo to become stars. The stages trace a career: pitching to a record label, concert halls, then overseas. You control both members at once. They copy each other's movements, and up and down change the gap between them. Their song attack, the 'charisma wave', freezes an enemy, and catching a frozen enemy between the two kills it and drops an item. Getting hit loses your stage-clear item or a gold disc before it costs a life. There are five stages and a hidden sixth, with buildings that need certain conditions to enter. Contemporary reviews were harsh.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action-based; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Exploration platformer: as Mikey, explore a sprawling network of caverns and the Fratellis' hideout, use items and first-person rooms to find six captured Goonies, then rescue the mermaid Annie.
dossier: Konami's sequel to its Famicom The Goonies, and an early non-linear exploration platformer in the vein of Castlevania II. It has a game-original story and character, the mermaid Annie. Mikey crosses a large map of 'front' and 'back' areas connected by ladders and warp rooms, fighting Fratelli family members and creatures with yo-yos, slingshots and bombs. Doors lead to first-person rooms where you search, use items and talk to people, which is how key items and clues are found. Each Goonie you rescue adds to your maximum life. Rescue all six to reach Annie and the ending. The Famicom text is entirely katakana.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The platforming is visual, but the first-person rooms involve katakana dialogue and item clues; progress is possible by experimenting.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as The Goonies II (1987).

gameplay_summary: Licensed action game starring Takara's Jenny doll: explore an overhead town map for the right stage entrances, then punch, kick and spray your way through side-scrolling stages to recover a stolen musical script.
dossier: A tie-in with Takara's Jenny fashion doll that is a tough action game rather than a girls' mini-game collection. The evil BB gang steals the script for Jenny's musical, and she goes after it herself. The overhead 'Mystery Town' map hides stage entrances at random, with a buzzer for wrong ones, and wandering enemies there can hurt you while you can't fight back. Inside the side-scrolling stages Jenny kicks and punches, and a limited spray gives ranged attacks. Hidden weapons can be found by specific actions. You clear six stages and collect the items that open the theatre. Tough enemies and vague hit detection make it hard, and one magazine joked it was Makaimura for girls.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action-based; the story text isn't needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Split-screen spy duel on a tropical island: dig pits, rig rope snares, coconuts and mines for your rival, fight him with stick or knife, and find the hidden missile parts and escape first.
dossier: Kemco's Famicom version of First Star's 1985 Spy vs. Spy II: The Island Caper, the sequel to Spy vs. Spy. The White and Black spies (Heckel and Jackel in the Japanese manual) race across a side-scrolling island to dig up missile parts and reach the escape point first. You build traps rather than starting with them: a shovel digs pits that need covering, rope snares and coconut drops are set in palm trees, and buried mines look just like the holes holding missile parts. This time traps cost life instead of killing outright, and the two spies share one timer. When they meet, they fight, and a stick or knife makes you stronger. It's best with two players.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Visual action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. An NES version (Spy vs. Spy: The Island Caper) was planned but never released, and the earlier NES Spy vs. Spy is the first game (FC-0117).

gameplay_summary: Comedy murder-mystery adventure: as comedian Sanma Akashiya's assistant, question a cast of real Yoshimoto comedians and search locations with command menus to solve a killing and a diamond theft.
dossier: A Namco command-menu adventure starring Sanma Akashiya and other real Yoshimoto Kogyo comedians, which entered Famitsu's Gold Hall of Fame. At a party at the Yoshimoto president's villa, comedian Bunchin Katsura is found dead in the vault and a diamond is missing. You move around a map, then investigate with commands such as Call, Ask, Search, Evidence and Memo. There's also a 'Sanma' command to let him take the lead, and a 'Doku' (smack) command. Searching offers verbs like hit, push, open and eat, plus a crab cursor for pointing anywhere. Animated characters, gags, mini-games and a little cheeky content keep it lively. Several endings exist, and only one catches the real culprit.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A dialogue-driven mystery full of Japanese comedy; understanding what suspects say is essential.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
